title: Called to beatitude (CCC 1716–1729)
hookLine: the beatitudes describe the happiness God wants for us

cards: The Catechism's part on how Catholics live could have started with a list of rules. It doesn't. It turns to a mountain, a crowd, and one word said again and again: blessed.
Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are the meek. Blessed are they that mourn.

Before any instruction about what to avoid, Jesus describes people who are, in his word, blessed. Some don't look it at all: the grieving, the hungry and thirsty, the persecuted. A surprise about who is happy.

teach.b: Back on day three hundred twelve, you met the beatitudes as a portrait of Jesus. The Catechism calls them the heart of Jesus's preaching.
In the Douay-Rheims the first reads: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

teach.h: A DESIRE FOR HAPPINESS, FROM GOD.
teach.b: Some readers hear blessed as happy, and the Catechism comes close: the beatitudes, it says, answer the natural desire for happiness, a desire that comes from God, placed in the heart to draw people to himself.
Saint Augustine, quoted there, asks God: how is it that I seek you? Because in seeking you, I seek the happy life. So morality here doesn't start with what's forbidden.
It starts with what a person wants most, and the claim that God wants it for them too. Then the beatitudes turn that wanting around.

True happiness, the Catechism says, isn't found in riches or comfort, fame or power, or any human achievement, however useful. It names the goal: the coming of the kingdom, the vision of God, entering into God's rest.
"Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God."
And the beatitudes show the face of Jesus Christ.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.
teach.b: They describe him first, the poor one, the meek one, the one who mourned, and then the happiness held out to anyone who follows. So the question shifts: not only what am I allowed to do, but what am I made for.
The beatitudes put decisive choices in front of a person, and everything in this part of the book, the commandments included, comes after that.

how: Catholics hear the beatitudes from Matthew 5 read at Mass, and the Catechism places them near the start of its teaching on the moral life, before the commandments.

o: a reward for keeping every rule perfectly
a feeling of pleasure that comes and goes
the blessed happiness God made people for

games.q: a friend asks where a guide to how Christians live ought to begin. by the Catechism's own order, what comes first?
o: with the rules that must never be broken.
with the happiness people are made for.
with a checklist of good habits.
games.why: the Catechism's part on the moral life opens with human dignity, and almost at once turns to the beatitudes and the call to beatitude. the commandments come later.

practice: Start with the surface wants, a quieter week, a bit more money, and let them go by. Then ask underneath: if I had all of those, what would I still want?
Keep asking until you reach something you can't buy, to be known, to be at peace, to love someone well, and if you pray, hold that desire up to God; if you don't, just stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Called to beatitude. Beatitude means blessedness, a happiness that comes as a gift. The Catechism says the human person is called to it, and that the beatitudes show the way. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: blessed, happy — the word that opens each beatitude in Matthew 5.

carryVoice: Your line: made for happiness. The longing comes before the rules, not after. See you tomorrow.
